content.overview: A percentage is only comparable when its numerator, denominator, stage, observation date and exclusions mean the same thing. Specialists define metrics before using them to judge a batch or process.

vocabulary.definition: A traceable group that entered a defined stage under a common batch definition.
Excluding or ending observation for units without silently changing the original denominator.

sections.title: Define the event and denominator
sections.body: Rooted, survived, released and handed off are different events. A metric should state which event occurred, the original eligible count and any documented exclusions.

sections.title: Observation windows change apparent performance
sections.body: A slower genotype can look worse at day 10 and equivalent at day 16. Compare like windows or present a time-to-event distribution rather than one arbitrary snapshot.

sections.title: Averages can hide batch structure
sections.body: Pooled results can conceal donor, genotype, operator, zone or time-period effects. Preserve batch-level records before calculating summaries.

workedExamples: Reporting 90 rooted plants out of the 95 still present inflates performance if the batch started with 110 and losses were removed.
Two lines with the same final rooting proportion can have very different time-to-root distributions and scheduling risk.
commonMistakes: Comparing different observation days as equivalent.
Pooling genotypes before checking batch-level variation.
content.practicalApplication: Audit a mock propagation dashboard, reconstruct every denominator and observation window, then rewrite three ambiguous KPIs as reproducible metric definitions.
content.summary: Reliable propagation metrics preserve cohorts, denominators, timing and exclusions so trends can be reproduced and compared.
